One Table, Many Queries: Benchmarking Generalist Tabular Models
Across Generation, Imputation, and Prediction

Yuanrui Wang Kaifang Li Xuanyue Li Ziyun Li Yan Lu Affiliation: StableAI Affiliation: Tsinghua University Affiliation: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications Affiliation: Southeast University Email: wangyuanrui@stable-ai.cn    Peng Cui Affiliation: StableAI Affiliation: Tsinghua University
Abstract

Generation, imputation, and prediction query different aspects of the same tabular distribution, but are usually evaluated separately. This leaves unclear which capabilities they share, how their training objectives interact, and whether one model can perform all three well. We introduce the One Table Benchmark (OTBench), spanning 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 capability axes under aligned data splits and explicit task contracts. We compare task ranks on aligned support, train five backbones under all seven non-empty objective combinations on five datasets with three seeds, and contrast fixed-model profiles with specialist portfolios. Rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility; distributional fidelity follows different, sometimes opposing, rankings. Objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from including the recipient’s own objective. Generation has the broadest coverage of positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility, with responses that vary across backbones. Cross-addition effects reveal that objective benefits need not add and depend on the objectives already present. Fixed-model comparisons expose corresponding utility–fidelity trade-offs: some generalists surpass specialist portfolios on utility, while fidelity continues to favor specialization. Frozen foundation models show strong prediction and numerical point imputation, together with promising synthetic-data utility, highlighting their potential across all three tasks. These findings motivate unified tabular models that share useful conditional information while improving categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling. Code is available at https://github.com/limix-ldm-ai/OTBench.

11footnotetext: Equal contribution.22footnotetext: Corresponding authors.

1 Introduction

Generation, imputation, and prediction use different aspects of the same tabular distribution. Generation produces complete records, imputation recovers missing features from observed information, and prediction infers a designated target. Each task has its own benchmarks and modeling traditions (Yang et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025; Erickson et al., 2025), yet their common statistical foundation suggests opportunities for sharing learned capabilities. Understanding these relationships matters for building models that can serve several uses of a table, and for deciding when a task should benefit from training on another.

The conditional-query view makes this connection explicit: generation queries the joint distribution, while imputation and prediction query feature and target conditionals. Models increasingly support several of these interfaces (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024; Zhang and others, 2025), but existing task-wise evaluations provide limited insight into which capabilities are shared. Appendix  reviews related benchmarks and generalist models.

Similar rankings may reflect useful common information without showing whether one training objective helps another. Conversely, objectives that help separately may provide overlapping or competing benefits when combined. We therefore study three questions: which capabilities co-occur across tasks, how objective additions and combinations affect a recipient task, and whether one fixed model can offer a competitive three-task profile.

We introduce the One Table Benchmark (OTBench), a unified platform for these comparisons. It covers 56 datasets, 46 registered methods, and 20 semantic capability axes. A common outer train–test split aligns the data populations across tasks, while explicit information-access and missingness contracts preserve each task’s meaning. Metric analysis separates point accuracy, distributional fidelity, dependence preservation, predictive quality, and downstream utility, so that cross-task relationships can be located at the level of capabilities. Figure  summarizes the benchmark workflow.

We first compare task ranks on aligned method–dataset support (Section ). Imputation and prediction agree most consistently through numerical recovery, dependence preservation, and predictive utility. Generation connects to both through the predictive utility of synthetic data, whereas distributional fidelity has different, sometimes opposing, rank relationships. This suggests that the information needed for useful conditional queries can be shared even when broader distributional criteria favor different methods.

To examine objective contributions under controlled changes, we train five backbones under all seven non-empty combinations of generation, imputation, and prediction on five datasets with three seeds and declared inference policies (Section ). Single-addition effects (SAE) measure the gain from enabling one objective; cross-addition effects (CAE) measure whether two objectives contribute additively. Recipient self-inclusion yields the largest pooled gains. Generation has broadly positive pooled auxiliary effects, while prediction shows potential to improve imputation and synthetic-data utility. These pooled auxiliary responses are descriptive and backbone-dependent. CAE reveals sub-additivity and context dependence on the benchmark rank scale: useful individual objectives need not yield additive joint gains.

Finally, fixed-model profiles and comparisons with declared specialist portfolios connect these relationships to practical model choice (Section ). Fidelity and utility favor different profiles; no fixed identity leads throughout. Recent tabular foundation models (Zhang and others, 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Grinsztajn and others, 2026) achieve strong prediction and numerical point imputation without single-dataset fine-tuning, and their generation is competitive on downstream utility. These results reveal potential for unified foundation models, while motivating better categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    A conditional-query benchmark that aligns datasets and capability axes across generation, imputation, and prediction while preserving task-specific information and evaluation contracts;

  • •

    Complementary rank comparisons, matched objective interventions, and fixed-model profile experiments that distinguish shared capabilities, objective interactions, and practical generality;

  • •

    Empirical findings on utility-centered task relationships, non-additive objective effects, and the potential of foundation models to support all three tasks.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Definition

To compare methods within a common probabilistic framework, we formulate generation, imputation, and prediction as queries to the same joint distribution over a table. Let a complete row be Z=(X1,…,Xp,Y)∈𝒵:=(∏j=1𝒳j)×𝒴Z=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{p},Y)\in\mathcal{Z}:=\bigl(\prod_{j=1}\mathcal{X}_{j}\bigr)\times\mathcal{Y}, where X=(X1,…,Xp)X=(X_{1},\ldots,X_{p}) denotes the features, YY denotes the supervised target, and 𝒵\mathcal{Z} is the Cartesian product of their domains. Each variable may be continuous or discrete. We denote the unknown joint distribution of ZZ by ℙ\mathbb{P}. Let ℐ={1,…,p}\mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,p\} and 𝒱=ℐ∪{p+1}\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{I}\cup\{p+1\}, with Zp+1=YZ_{p+1}=Y. We represent each task as q=(O,Q,C)q=(O,Q,C), where O,Q⊆𝒱O,Q\subseteq\mathcal{V}, O∩Q=∅O\cap Q=\varnothing, and CC specifies the task protocol. Given fitted parameters θ^\hat{\theta}, the model approximates ℙ⁡(ZQ∣ZO;C)\mathbb{P}(Z_{Q}\mid Z_{O};C) by ℙ^θ^​(ZQ∣ZO;C)\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\hat{\theta}}(Z_{Q}\mid Z_{O};C). Table  summarizes the observed variables, queried variables, and target distribution for each task. For imputation, M⊆ℐM\subseteq\mathcal{I} denotes the masked feature set, with TC={p+1}T_{C}=\{p+1\} when the target is visible under protocol CC and TC=∅T_{C}=\varnothing otherwise.

2.2 Dataset Construction

Before evaluating any method, we construct a 56-dataset benchmark from 492 OpenML datasets (Vanschoren et al., 2013) reported across 24 studies. We apply prespecified feasibility filters, then use method-independent descriptors for PCA and kk-means (Jolliffe, 2002; Lloyd, 1982). The nearest nonduplicate candidate to each of 50 centroids forms the OpenML track, while six TabStruct structural-causal-model datasets (Jiang et al., 2026) form a separate structural track. Dataset selection does not use results from any evaluated method. All tasks share a fixed train–test split, and model fitting, preprocessing, schema estimation, and model selection use the training split only. Appendix  details sources, matching, filtering, descriptors, clustering, duplicate suppression, aggregate benchmark composition, the fixed split, and the separate SCM track.

3 Evaluation Metrics

3.1 Common-support rank protocol

Let xs,m,kx_{s,m,k} be the replicate-averaged value of metric kk for method mm in stratum ss. We orient it using ϕk​(x)∈{x,−x,−|x−ak|}\phi_{k}(x)\in\{x,-x,-|x-a_{k}|\} for higher-is-better, error, or target-proximity metrics. For collection cc with members 𝒦c\mathcal{K}_{c}, let ℳs,c\mathcal{M}_{s,c} contain methods with observations for every member:

rs,m,k=prankm∈ℳs,c⁡(ϕk​(xs,m,k)),Ss,m,c=1|𝒦c|​∑k∈𝒦crs,m,k.r_{s,m,k}=\operatorname{prank}_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{s,c}}\!\left(\phi_{k}(x_{s,m,k})\right),\qquad S_{s,m,c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{c}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{c}}r_{s,m,k}. (1)

Ties receive the average percentile rank, and Ss,m,cS_{s,m,c} requires all declared members. A metric pair c={i,j}c=\{i,j\} is used to audit redundancy; a retained axis cc defines an axis score. Both use the same orientation and common support within separate protocol strata; full details are in Appendix . All subsequent analyses keep the same fixed member set 𝒦c\mathcal{K}_{c} and the same member-complete, equal-weight aggregation rule. Their ranking reference populations remain analysis-specific: for example, Task Rank Analysis ranks within a task pair’s aligned common-method support, whereas Controlled Transfer ranks within the seven objective arms.

3.2 Redundancy and retained axes

Redundancy occurs in every task but varies in extent: generation retains the richest local structure, whereas prediction shows the greatest compression (Table ). PCA shows stronger global compression, but a shared latent direction does not imply that two metrics are substitutable.

The audit therefore informs axis construction without mechanically determining it. We merge only aligned metrics that share an estimand, preserve distinct or opposing quantities, and keep the components of diagnostic bundles available for separate reporting. This yields 20 semantic axes; protocol strata remain separate rather than being counted as new constructs. Table  records their exact membership; Appendix  gives the task-specific rationales alongside Figures – . Axis scores remain separate rather than forming a universal score.

Where applicable, our metric definitions follow established constructions. Marginal-shape errors combine per-column two-sample KS statistics for numerical variables (Smirnov, 1948) with categorical total-variation distances. We also use C2ST (Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017); α\alpha-precision, β\beta-recall, and authenticity (Alaa et al., 2022); a mixed-type kk-way query workload adapted from discrete marginal queries (McKenna et al., 2019); and a TSTR gap adapted from the TSTR protocol (Esteban et al., 2017). The privacy axis combines benchmark-defined closest-record diagnostics based on Gower distance (Gower, 1971), a distance-based membership diagnostic motivated by membership-inference attacks and low-FPR reporting  (Shokri et al., 2017; Carlini et al., 2022), and a legacy δ\delta-presence-inspired diagnostic (Nergiz et al., 2007); none constitutes a privacy guarantee. The imputation distribution axes use Jensen–Shannon divergence (Lin, 1991) and the 1-Wasserstein distance (Villani, 2009). Classification evaluation includes balanced accuracy and MCC (Brodersen et al., 2010; Matthews, 1975), ROC-AUC and average precision (Hanley and McNeil, 1982; Davis and Goadrich, 2006), proper scores (Brier, 1950; Good, 1952), and calibration and selective-prediction measures (Naeini et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2017; Geifman et al., 2019).

4 Task Rank Analysis

4.1 Objective and Method

To characterize cross-task alignment among existing methods, we compare their relative rankings across generation (G), imputation (I), and prediction (P). Consistent rankings would indicate that the evaluated capabilities covary across tasks, whereas axis-dependent or conflicting rankings would show that cross-task performance cannot be adequately summarized by a single score.

Training protocol.

Cross-task rank analysis requires a method to support multiple tasks. We therefore select models with benchmark interfaces for at least two of G, I, and P; Table 7 lists the methods and their supported tasks. Each model follows its default training or adaptation protocol, including its prescribed pretrained or in-context route where applicable. Dataset-specific fitting and adaptation use the training split of each OTBench dataset, and evaluation uses its held-out test split. The same outer split is shared across tasks, so task comparisons do not change the underlying training and test populations. Appendix  gives the model configurations.

For each task pair aa and bb, we identify the common method pool ℳa​b\mathcal{M}_{ab}, align metric directions, average scores over seeds or replicates, and analyze classification and regression separately. Imputation uses the target-observed, missing-completely-at-random (MCAR) setting (Rubin, 1976) with a missing rate of 0.30.3.

Capability-axis scores follow the common-support rank protocol in Section . For each axis pair c,cc,c and dataset dd, we retain methods in ℳa​b\mathcal{M}_{ab} for which all declared members of both axes are valid. We orient the metrics and compute percentile ranks on this aligned method set, then aggregate the member ranks according to Equation . The ranking reference set is specific to each task pair and axis pair.

We compute one pooled Spearman correlation (Spearman, 1904) over the aligned dataset–method units. To assess sensitivity to method-pool composition, we perform leave-one-method-out (LOMO) analysis by removing each method in turn and recomputing the aligned support, within-dataset ranks, axis scores, and pooled correlation. An axis pair is LOMO-direction-preserving only when every effective deletion preserves the sign of the full-pool correlation; deletions that change no valid unit are excluded from this diagnostic. Appendix  gives the full construction.

4.2 Results and Discussion

Cross-task rank agreement depends on the capability axes being compared (Figure ). No uniform correspondence holds across all tasks and evaluation dimensions.

Imputation–prediction.

Imputation and prediction show selective rank agreement, with 13 of the 24 classification axis pairs and 14 of the 18 regression pairs preserving direction under LOMO. Across both prediction settings, numerical point accuracy, association, and downstream utility gap have positive, direction-preserving correlations with every prediction axis. The distributional axes show a different pattern. Numerical distribution maintains positive agreement with all three regression axes, but neither distribution axis has a direction-preserving relationship with classification performance.

Recovering values for individual records and preserving variable relationships can retain information useful for target prediction. This is consistent with our intuition that learned statistical dependencies can support both imputation and prediction. Matching marginal value distributions emphasizes a different property of the completed data, which helps explain its less uniform correspondence with prediction. The connection is more direct for downstream utility gap because it evaluates completion quality through predictive performance. Together, these results locate the shared performance of imputation and prediction in numerical recovery, dependence preservation, and predictive utility. For unified models, this suggests a focus on learning relationships that support both missing-feature recovery and target prediction, including when the target itself is unavailable as conditioning information.

Generation–imputation.

Generation and imputation have the highest proportion of LOMO-direction-preserving relationships among the task pairs, with 36 of the 42 axis pairs preserving direction. TSTR gap and global-utility compromise show positive, direction-preserving correlations with all six imputation axes. Privacy-risk diagnostics show negative, direction-preserving correlations with every imputation axis except numerical distribution.

TSTR gap measures the preservation of target-specific predictive utility relative to predictors trained on real data. Its positive rank correlations indicate that generation methods whose synthetic data better preserve this utility also tend to rank higher on imputation. This is consistent with our intuition that learned variable dependencies can support both useful data generation and missing-value recovery. Fidelity and C2ST assess marginal and low-order statistical similarity and real–synthetic distinguishability, respectively, and their correlations with imputation axes vary in sign. Thus, both tasks can use dependencies among table variables, but a method that ranks highly on generation metrics does not necessarily lead on imputation. Whether its advantage carries over depends on how effectively the learned relationships support recovery of missing values from observed information.

Generation–prediction.

For generation and prediction, 17 of the 28 classification axis pairs and 9 of the 21 regression axis pairs preserve direction under LOMO. Fidelity and C2ST show negative, direction-preserving correlations with all four classification axes, whereas TSTR gap and global-utility compromise show positive, direction-preserving correlations with all classification and regression axes.

This contrast in correlation signs distinguishes the statistical similarity of synthetic data from their predictive utility. Prediction relies on conditional information relevant to a specified target, while generation evaluation also examines other distributional properties whose importance to that target can vary. The shared focus of TSTR gap and the prediction axes on target-related information helps explain their positive rank agreement. These results connect generation and prediction through the preservation of target-specific predictive utility. Future work could explicitly model target-relevant dependencies in generation and assess their effects on predictive utility and distributional fidelity.

5 From Rank Alignment to Causal Transfer

Section  characterizes relationships among tasks through the agreement of method rankings on matched capability axes. This reveals which capabilities tend to co-occur across methods, but leaves open how the tasks contribute to one another within a model: architectures, training protocols, and objective combinations vary together in those comparisons. To examine these relationships under controlled changes, we ask whether adding an objective improves another recipient task, and whether objectives combine additively within a shared model. We call this experiment causal transfer: matched interventions on the enabled objectives complement the observational evidence from task ranks.

Experimental setup and evaluation.

We train Gaussian Copula (Patki et al., 2016), Forest-VP Joint (Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024), TabDiff (Shi et al., 2025), TabSyn (Zhang et al., 2024), and TabDDPM (Kotelnikov et al., 2023) under all seven non-empty objective arms 𝒞={G,I,P,G​I,G​P,I​P,G​I​P}\mathcal{C}=\{G,I,P,GI,GP,IP,GIP\}. The study uses five datasets—JapaneseVowels, cleveland, credit_card_clients_default, website_phishing, and MiamiHousing2016—and training seeds {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}, yielding 525 backbone–dataset–seed–arm systems. The first four datasets are classification problems and the last is regression. We use the fixed OTBench training and test splits, hold the configured training budget fixed across arms within each backbone, and sample enabled objectives uniformly during fitting. G scores all table variables; I reconstructs randomly selected features with the target hidden; P predicts the target from the features. The neural pipelines reserve an internal validation split from the training data, and TabSyn shares an objective-independent VAE across the seven arms of each dataset–seed block.

Each trained system is evaluated on all three tasks. Generation produces as many synthetic rows as the outer training split; TSTR fits a predictor on these rows and evaluates it on held-out real data, with a real-trained predictor as reference. Imputation evaluates held-out feature recovery under MCAR, MAR, MNAR, and mixed missingness at rates {0.1,0.3,0.5}\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}, using three completed-table draws per fixed, method-independent mask and keeping the target hidden. Prediction evaluates held-out targets, aggregating three conditional draws for the four diffusion-based backbones; Gaussian Copula uses its native Monte Carlo query. Comparisons match backbone, dataset, training seed, and atomic evaluation setting. Within each matched block, we orient each metric so that higher is better, normalize its seven-arm ranks to [0,1][0,1], and average member ranks within each capability axis. Every member must be finite for all seven arms. Imputation contrasts are formed separately for each mechanism–rate setting before equally weighted aggregation; classification and regression axes remain separate. Intervals use 2,000 crossed backbone–dataset bootstrap draws with seed resampling. Appendix  gives the splits, training configurations, sampling budgets, and unavailable outcomes; Appendix  specifies matching and uncertainty.

5.1 Single-addition effect (SAE)

Let SA,aS_{A,a} denote the normalized score on recipient axis aa for objective arm AA, suppressing the matched block indices. For source objective ss, recipient task tt, and remaining task uu, the single-addition effect is

SAEs→t,a=12​[(Ss​t,a−St,a)+(Ss​t​u,a−St​u,a)],{s,t,u}={G,I,P}.\operatorname{SAE}_{s\rightarrow t,a}=\frac{1}{2}\left[(S_{st,a}-S_{t,a})+(S_{stu,a}-S_{tu,a})\right],\qquad\{s,t,u\}=\{G,I,P\}. (2)

It averages the gain from adding ss when uu is absent and present, with the recipient objective included on both sides. A positive value indicates an improvement on the recipient axis. For self-inclusion, the added objective and recipient coincide: we instead average its addition to the three non-empty arms formed from the other two objectives. No empty training arm is required. For the diffusion-based backbones, I/P inference uses clean observed features (x0x_{0}) when that recipient objective is enabled and the xtx_{t} conditioning path otherwise; Gaussian Copula always uses native conditioning. Off-diagonal SAE therefore fixes the recipient’s inference rule, whereas I/P self-inclusion compares complete training–inference systems. Generation inference is fixed throughout.

Direct supervision gives the largest gains.

Self-inclusion is positive on all 19 displayed axes and exceeds both auxiliary-objective effects on each axis (Figure ). Its effects range from .122.122 to .445.445 for generation, .159.159 to .317.317 for imputation, and .098.098 to .456.456 for prediction. Thus, explicitly training for the recipient is the strongest direct intervention in this study. This supports including the desired task’s own objective as a first priority; it does not imply that a singleton arm always outperforms every joint arm.

Generation provides broadly positive auxiliary effects.

Beyond self-inclusion, G has the broadest positive coverage: its pooled SAE is positive on all six imputation axes and five of seven prediction axes. The exceptions are regression squared error and mean absolute error. Generation requires fitting values across the joint table distribution, which may encourage representations of dependencies useful to several conditional queries. Its broad modeling scope offers a possible explanation for this pattern, rather than evidence that generation is intrinsically the hardest task or uniformly beneficial.

Both G and P improve the pooled means on every imputation axis. P has the larger effect on four of six axes, including numerical point accuracy (.080.080 versus .007.007) and association (.105.105 versus .082.082); G is stronger on the two distributional axes. One possible explanation concerns the heterogeneity of reconstruction targets. Some features are weakly predictable from the observed variables, so their reconstruction losses can provide limited conditional signal. I trains on smaller queried subsets, where such features may account for a larger share of the update than in G, which scores the whole row. P concentrates supervision on a designated prediction target and may supply a more consistent conditional learning signal that also helps feature recovery. These are hypotheses about the observed pattern; we do not measure feature predictability or gradient alignment, and a supervised target need not be fully predictable.

Prediction can improve the downstream utility of generated data.

Adding P to G produces a larger positive response on the normalized TSTR-gap score (.092.092) than on the global-utility composite (−.008-.008), motivating the closer view in Figure . TSTR evaluates a central use of synthetic data: training predictors that generalize to real records. A higher TSTR-gap score means a gap closer to the real-trained reference, not a change of the same magnitude in raw predictive accuracy. Four of five backbones have positive P→\rightarrowG TSTR-gap rank effects, with Forest-VP Joint the exception (−.033-.033). The pooled interval remains wide ([−.041,.225][-.041,.225]). Auxiliary per-column diagnostics also suggest a stronger response at the designated target than across all columns, although the paired localization contrasts are inconclusive. Prediction-oriented supervision is therefore a promising strategy for improving synthetic-data utility, with benefits that depend on the backbone and evaluation axis. The off-diagonal patterns here are descriptive: none meets the complete cross-backbone robustness criterion, which is reported alongside the uncertainty estimates rather than used to discard their differing responses.

5.2 Cross-addition effect (CAE)

To measure whether objectives combine additively, we define the cross-addition effect for added objectives s,ts,t and anchor uu:

CAEs×t|u,a=(Ss​t​u,a−Ss​u,a)−(St​u,a−Su,a),{s,t,u}={G,I,P}.\operatorname{CAE}_{s\times t\mid u,a}=(S_{stu,a}-S_{su,a})-(S_{tu,a}-S_{u,a}),\qquad\{s,t,u\}=\{G,I,P\}. (3)

Here the recipient is determined by axis aa and may differ from the anchor. A positive CAE means that the score increment from adding tt is larger when ss is already present (complementarity); a negative CAE means that its increment is smaller (sub-additivity). A zero value is consistent with additive effects on this rank scale. Sub-additivity does not require either added objective to be harmful on its own.

Objective interactions depend on context.

Figure  shows sub-additivity for G×I|PG\times I\mid P across all six non-privacy generation axes and all six imputation axes, and for G×P|IG\times P\mid I across all seven prediction axes. Seven G–I effects meet the full robustness criterion. With G as the anchor, I×P|GI\times P\mid G instead has positive means on all six imputation and five of seven prediction axes, consistent with the P→\rightarrowI SAE pattern; however, these intervals cross zero. Joint gains therefore depend on the recipient and objective context. Shared information may yield overlap or complementarity, while fixed budgets may create update or capacity competition. These mechanisms remain hypotheses, and I/P interactions that toggle the recipient also include its conditioning-policy switch.

5.3 Objective-arm Pareto profiles

CAE describes interactions on individual capability axes. We next examine the resulting three-task trade-offs among the seven training arms. Figure  uses available coordinates across all five backbones: within each block, retained axes and imputation settings must be scored for all seven arms. Settings are averaged within axes, then retained non-privacy axes are equally weighted; seeds, datasets within each backbone, and backbones are averaged successively. Different blocks may retain different axes.

All three task coordinates are oriented so that higher is better. An arm exactly dominates another if it is no worse on any coordinate and strictly better on at least one. Material dominance requires no loss on any coordinate and a gain of at least ϵ=.05\epsilon=.05 on at least one. The exact frontier and material frontier consist of arms not dominated by any other candidate under the respective rule. Both are computed jointly in (G,I,P)(G,I,P), rather than separately in pairwise projections.

The exact and material frontiers both contain {G,G​I,G​P,I​P,G​I​P}\{G,GI,GP,IP,GIP\}. In the pooled estimates, GP has the strongest generation coordinate, IP the strongest imputation coordinate, and GIP the strongest prediction coordinate. GIP combines high I/P scores with a lower G coordinate than GP, and has 94%94\% exact-frontier bootstrap membership. This is a competitive compromise, rather than universal superiority. Support also matters: the complete-block analysis (47 blocks) retains only {G​I,G​P,G​I​P}\{GI,GP,GIP\} (Appendix ). These objective-arm trade-offs lead to the next section’s comparison of fixed, deployable method identities with specialist portfolios.

6 Fixed-Method Generality

We now compare fixed model identities across tasks and ask when one generalist is competitive with a specialist portfolio. Each method retains the same identity across datasets, capability axes, and missingness settings. Comparisons preserve the task contracts and percentile composites in Equation ; no method switches identities to assemble an oracle.

Performance rankings depend on the capability axis.

Figure  reports the fraction of contract-compatible fixed specialists beaten by each generalist, averaged over paired datasets with half credit for ties. Imputation comparisons are computed separately in each of the twelve target-observed mechanism–rate settings before averaging. These fractions describe relative position, not raw accuracy.

Generation shows a clear separation between distributional fidelity and predictive utility: Gaussian Copula leads fidelity, C2ST, and α\alpha-precision, Forest-VP Joint leads association, and TabPFN-3 leads the TSTR-gap axis and global-utility composite. Imputation is similarly divided: TabPFN-3 leads numerical point accuracy, TabICLv2 leads numerical distribution, association, and utility preservation, and TabSyn leads both categorical axes. LimiX-2 leads every displayed prediction axis. Thus, competence on one criterion does not imply a matching advantage on other criteria, even within the same task.

Joint profiles expose different bottlenecks and trade-offs.

Figure (a)–(c) connects each method’s G, I, and P coordinates under three prespecified profiles. Numerical fidelity combines generation fidelity, numerical imputation point accuracy, and regression squared error; categorical fidelity substitutes categorical imputation point accuracy and classification hard decisions; downstream utility combines generation TSTR, imputation utility preservation, and classification hard decisions. Each profile uses its own common dataset cohort. Its percentile-composite coordinates differ from the specialist-beating fractions in Figure .

High prediction and numerical imputation can coexist with weaker generation fidelity, while several generative methods show the opposite imbalance. Categorical reconstruction introduces another bottleneck, and the utility profile produces a different, often more balanced ordering. These contrasts show why a single cross-task average would obscure useful distinctions. The practical Pareto frontier (ϵ=.05\epsilon=.05) contains LimiX-2 and TabDDPM for numerical fidelity; Gaussian Copula, TabDDPM, TabDiff, and TabPFN-3 for categorical fidelity; and LimiX-2, TabDDPM, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3 for utility. No fixed identity is uniformly best across the three profiles.

Specialist portfolios retain a fidelity advantage.

Figure (d)–(f) compares each generalist with one declared specialist triple per profile (Appendix ), using paired differences in worst-task percentile. The numerical-fidelity portfolio outperforms every generalist. The categorical portfolio also has higher mean performance throughout: generalist-minus-portfolio gaps range from −.396-.396 to −.261-.261, with all bootstrap intervals below zero, although this cohort contains only three datasets. Utility yields a different conclusion. TabICLv2 exceeds its portfolio by .157.157 (95%95\% CI [.078,.229][.078,.229]) and TabPFN-3 by .142.142 ([.051,.227][.051,.227]). LimiX-2’s interval spans zero, while the remaining methods have negative mean gaps. Generalist deployment is therefore most competitive for the evaluated utility profile; fidelity-oriented workloads continue to benefit from specialization. Appendix  gives the setting-specific comparisons and statistical diagnostics.

Implications for foundation models.

LimiX-2, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3 achieve strong numerical point imputation and prediction without single-dataset fine-tuning, while their generation is more competitive on utility than fidelity. LimiX-2 includes masked-feature reconstruction, whereas TabICLv2 and TabPFN-3 reuse pretrained predictors through conditional imputation extensions (Zhang and others, 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Grinsztajn and others, 2026; Prior Labs, 2026). Categorical reconstruction on the common profile cohort and faithful joint generation remain limitations. Amid rapid progress and growing interest in tabular foundation models, these findings highlight their potential across all three tasks. We hope our results encourage foundation-model researchers to develop a unified model that excels at generation, imputation, and prediction.

7 Conclusion

OTBench provides a common setting for studying how generation, imputation, and prediction relate through their capabilities, training objectives, and fixed-model performance. Task-rank comparisons connect imputation and prediction through numerical recovery and dependence preservation, and link generation to both through predictive utility. Distributional fidelity follows different relationships, so task competence cannot be inferred from one criterion alone. Matched objective interventions show the largest pooled gains from recipient self-inclusion and suggest backbone-dependent auxiliary benefits from generation and prediction. Their benefits need not add: joint outcomes depend on the recipient and the objectives already present. Fixed-model profiles further show why utility and fidelity can favor different generalist or specialist choices.

Foundation models already demonstrate strong prediction and numerical point imputation without dataset-specific fine-tuning, together with promising synthetic-data utility. Amid rapid progress in this field, these findings highlight their potential across all three tasks. We hope OTBench encourages researchers to develop foundation models that excel at generation, imputation, and prediction, including reliable categorical reconstruction and faithful joint sampling.

8 Limitations and Future Work

Scope and comparability.

Our conclusions depend on the capability axes, information contracts, and available method–dataset support. Rank alignment describes capability co-occurrence, rather than identifying objective transfer. In particular, the rank study’s target-observed imputation and the controlled study’s target-hidden imputation provide complementary evidence under different contracts. Profile and portfolio comparisons also use different common cohorts; the categorical profile contains only three datasets. Cross-task imputation coordinates average twelve settings and do not replace setting-specific evaluation.

Objective effects and their mechanisms.

The factorial study covers five backbones and five datasets, with only one regression dataset and some unavailable evaluations. Auxiliary single-addition effects remain exploratory and heterogeneous across backbones. SAE and CAE quantify changes on a normalized rank scale; they do not identify the mechanisms behind those changes. I/P self-inclusion and some interaction comparisons can also change the conditioning policy, while fixed training budgets redistribute updates among objectives. Objective overlap, update allocation, capacity competition, and gradient interference therefore require separate interventions.

Directions for unified models.

The frozen foundation-model results establish the capabilities of the evaluated inference systems, without isolating the contribution of pretraining, representations, or decoders. Matched pretraining and inference ablations are needed before attributing categorical or generation gaps to specific backbone properties. Future work should broaden the dataset and model populations, separate training from inference effects, and test how categorical reconstruction and joint sampling can improve alongside prediction.

AI Use Statement

We used AI tools to assist with manuscript drafting and editing, figure preparation, and LaTeX formatting. The authors are responsible for the final manuscript and its scientific claims.

Reproducibility Statement

To facilitate reproducibility, we describe the task definitions in Section  and the evaluation and aggregation protocols in Section . Dataset sources, selection criteria, data splits, and preprocessing procedures are detailed in Appendix . Baseline configurations, hyperparameter settings and selection rules, random seeds, and computational resources are provided in Appendix . Metric definitions and result aggregation procedures are specified in Appendices  and , with analysis-specific protocols in Appendices –. Benchmark source code, method configurations, and evaluation routines are publicly available at https://github.com/limix-ldm-ai/OTBench.

Ethics Statement

This study evaluates tabular learning methods using publicly available datasets under their respective licenses and terms of use. We do not collect additional personal data or attempt to identify individuals in the datasets. We recognize that synthetic data may retain sensitive information from the training data, and that empirical privacy evaluations do not constitute formal privacy guarantees. Furthermore, aggregate benchmark performance does not establish fairness across demographic groups or suitability for deployment in high-stakes settings. Any downstream use should therefore be accompanied by application-specific assessments of privacy, fairness, and reliability.

Appendix A Dataset Construction Details

A.1 Construction Objective and Overall Pipeline

The benchmark supports prediction, missing-value imputation, and data generation under a controlled computational budget. Evaluating every candidate dataset would be costly and would overrepresent sources with multiple versions and groups of structurally similar datasets. We therefore select representative datasets using only method-independent dataset properties and fixed landmarking statistics (Pfahringer et al., 2000). All selection rules and configurations are specified before method evaluation begins, so no evaluated method’s performance influences dataset selection. Figure  summarizes the construction process, from the literature-derived candidate pool to the two final evaluation sets.

A.2 Literature-Driven Candidate Dataset Pool

We identify candidate datasets from 24 deduplicated literature source groups. These sources cover general tabular prediction benchmarks as well as specialized studies of missing-value imputation, data generation, structural fidelity, and robustness. Table  lists these sources. ForestDiffusion covers both generation and imputation and is counted once; the two relevant TALENT studies form one source group. Literature sources define only the candidate pool and do not determine the weights used for representative selection.

After normalizing dataset names and common aliases, we resolve dataset identities using Dataset IDs reported in papers or official configurations, Task IDs that can be mapped to specific versions, frozen identifiers in official benchmark suites, and metadata that agree in dataset name, size, task type, and original source. We merge references to the same Dataset ID across studies while retaining all source attributions. Records with the same name but different Dataset IDs, versions, or sizes are not merged automatically. This process yields 492 datasets with unambiguous OpenML Dataset IDs (Vanschoren et al., 2013).

A.3 Data Parsing and Hard Filtering

Column types and target columns.

Variable types follow the ARFF header rather than the appearance of the values. Nominal attributes are treated as categorical variables, whereas numeric, real, and integer attributes are treated as numerical variables. A string attribute is treated as categorical only when its cardinality does not exceed min⁡(50,0.2​Ni)\min(50,0.2N_{i}). Other free-text fields and all date/relational attributes are removed. Thus, PiP_{i} counts usable features after removing target columns and unsupported fields, rather than raw CSV columns.

We use the OpenML default_target_attribute field to identify the target whenever available. If this field is missing, the target is inferred in order from common names, including class, label, target, y, and outcome, or from a low-cardinality final column. Such cases are marked by target_inferred. A numerical final column is inferred as a classification target only when it has between 2 and 30 unique values and the sample size is at least 20 times the number of unique values. For multi-target datasets, only the first target is used to compute prediction-related meta-features, while the original number of targets is retained.

Size constraints.

To keep evaluation within a common computational budget, we impose the following constraints on each dataset 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i}:

100≤Ni≤100,000,Pi≤160,Ni​Pi≤10.100\leq N_{i}\leq 100{,}000,\qquad P_{i}\leq 160,\qquad N_{i}P_{i}\leq 10. (4)

The 492 source entries yield 469 datasets for size screening. The size constraints exclude 92 datasets, leaving 377 candidates. Figure (a) shows the filtering outcome in sample-size–feature-count space.

A.4 Dataset Meta-Feature Representation

We recompute 113 meta-features for each candidate dataset using a unified local extractor. The extractor includes reproducible PyMFE statistics (Alcobaça et al., 2020) and standard clustering diagnostics (Hopkins and Skellam, 1954; Rousseeuw, 1987). The four meta-feature groups serve only for interpretation and post hoc diagnostics; we assign no manual group weights. Table 5 reports the original counts and lists all dimensions retained after cleaning.

Sampling and failure handling.

Dataset size, missingness rates, missingness patterns, and the duplicate-row ratio are computed on the full dataset. Other computationally expensive statistics use a random sample of at most 10,000 records. For meta-feature computation, we impute missing numerical values with the median and fill entirely missing numerical columns with 0. Missing categorical values are encoded as __missing__. These operations apply only to meta-feature computation and leave the original data unchanged. Failures are handled separately in the PyMFE, clustering-structure, dependency-structure, and landmarking modules. If a module fails, only its dimensions are marked as missing.

Landmarking.

Following the landmarking principle (Pfahringer et al., 2000), we characterize target predictability with four fixed lightweight models: a logistic/ridge linear model, a depth-3 decision tree, 5-nearest neighbors, and a random forest with 100 trees (Hoerl and Kennard, 1970; Breiman et al., 1984; Cover and Hart, 1967; Breiman, 2001). Within each fold, numerical features are median-imputed and standardized. Categorical features are constant-imputed and one-hot encoded, with at most 20 categories retained per column. We remove records with missing targets and, for classification, classes with fewer than 6 samples. If more than 5,000 records remain, 5,000 are sampled without replacement using random seed 0, followed by three-fold cross-validation. This limit applies only to auxiliary meta-feature computation; the final dataset is not truncated. For a KK-class classification task and a regression task, respectively, the scores are

scls=clip⁡(BalAcc−1/K1−1/K,0,1),sreg=clip⁡(R,0,1).s_{\mathrm{cls}}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{BalAcc}-1/K}{1-1/K},0,1\right),\qquad s_{\mathrm{reg}}=\operatorname{clip}(R,0,1). (5)

These scores describe the dataset’s target structure and exclude the performance of all methods evaluated in this paper.

A.5 Meta-Feature Cleaning and Normalization

Of the raw meta-features, 28 PyMFE statistics depend directly on the original measurement units, including means, standard deviations, extrema, covariances, and raw eigenvalues. Another 11 PyMFE counts or ratios duplicate the logarithmic or proportional representations in group A. The features has_target and target_missing_ratio are nearly constant in the current candidate pool. Removing these 41 dimensions leaves 72 meta-features. We apply no further within-group correlation pruning. PCA summarizes the remaining correlated variation in a lower-dimensional representation.

For datasets without an identified target, missing group-D meta-features are imputed using the corresponding median over datasets with valid targets. All other missing values are imputed using the median of the corresponding dimension over the full candidate pool. Any meta-feature with more than 20% missing values would also be removed during preprocessing.

Meta-features with at most two observed unique values are standardized using a zz-score. All other dimensions are mapped to a standard normal distribution by a QuantileTransformer (Pedregosa et al., 2011) fitted with at most 200 quantiles, then clipped to [−3.5,3.5][-3.5,3.5]:

h~i​j=clip⁡[Φ⁡(F^j​(hi​j)),−3.5,3.5],\widetilde{h}_{ij}=\operatorname{clip}\!\left[\Phi\!\left(\widehat{F}_{j}(h_{ij})\right),-3.5,3.5\right], (6)

where F^j\widehat{F}_{j} denotes the quantile map fitted with at most 200 empirical quantiles. Of the 72 retained dimensions, 69 use quantile normalization and 3 binary task-type indicators use zz-score standardization.

A.6 PCA Representation, Clustering, and Representative Selection

PCA representation.

Let H∈ℝH\in\mathbb{R} denote the standardized candidate-dataset matrix. We fit PCA (Jolliffe, 2002) without whitening and choose the smallest dimension qq satisfying

q=min⁡{r:∑j=1λj∑j=1λj≥0.99}.q=\min\left\{r:\frac{\sum_{j=1}\lambda_{j}}{\sum_{j=1}\lambda_{j}}\geq 0.99\right\}. (7)

This gives q=41q=41 and 99.0726% cumulative explained variance. The 41 principal components (PCs) are linear combinations of the 72 meta-features, not a subset of 41 original features. Figure (b) plots the cumulative explained variance against the number of PCs and marks the 41-component cutoff required to reach the 99% threshold.

Clustering and representative datasets.

Let 𝐞i∈ℝ\mathbf{e}_{i}\in\mathbb{R} denote the PCA coordinates of dataset 𝒟i\mathcal{D}_{i}. We apply kk-means (Lloyd, 1982) in this space with k=50k=50, n_init=10=10, and random seed 0. The clustering objective is

min⁡∑i=1{ai},{𝝁c}⁡‖𝐞i−𝝁ai‖2.\min_{\{a_{i}\},\{\bm{\mu}_{c}\}}\sum_{i=1}\left\|\mathbf{e}_{i}-\bm{\mu}_{a_{i}}\right\|_{2}. (8)

Clusters are processed in decreasing order of size. Within each cluster, we select the candidate nearest to the centroid among those allowed by the same-source rule. Let ℰc\mathcal{E}_{c} denote the set of eligible nonduplicate candidates when cluster cc is processed. The selected representative is

𝒟c=arg⁡min𝒟i∈Cc∩ℰc⁡‖𝐞i−𝝁c‖2.\mathcal{D}_{c}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{D}_{i}\in C_{c}\cap\mathcal{E}_{c}}\left\|\mathbf{e}_{i}-\bm{\mu}_{c}\right\|_{2}. (9)

The representative is an observed candidate dataset; the synthetic centroid cannot be evaluated directly.

Same-source version suppression.

Dataset names are converted to lowercase and stripped of nonalphanumeric characters. Two datasets are marked as potential versions of the same source if their normalized names are identical, or if the shorter normalized name has at least 5 characters and is a prefix of the other, provided that their sample counts differ by no more than a factor of 1.5. After one version is selected, other versions from the same source cannot represent later clusters. This procedure excludes 31 potential duplicates and selects one representative from each of the 50 clusters. Figure  shows a two-dimensional UMAP projection (McInnes et al., 2018) of the candidate datasets and selected representatives.

A.7 Final Benchmark, Data Splits, and Structural Evaluation Set

OpenML evaluation set.

The 50 selected OpenML-hosted datasets comprise 26 binary-classification, 9 multiclass-classification, and 15 regression datasets. By source type, 40 datasets are real-world or derived from real-world data, 9 are synthetic, simulated, or manually constructed, and 1 combines real and synthetic data. Task type and source type are separate classification schemes. The datasets contain 106–53,940 samples and 4–126 features. The largest table has 690,000 cells, and 8 datasets contain native missing values.

Fixed train–test split.

Dataset selection is completed before the final train–test split. Let 𝒟i={zi​j}j=1\mathcal{D}_{i}=\{z_{ij}\}_{j=1} have sample-index set Ii={1,…,Ni}I_{i}=\{1,\ldots,N_{i}\}. We define:

𝒟i,train={zi​j:j∈Ii,train},\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{i,\mathrm{train}}=\{z_{ij}:j\in I_{i,\mathrm{train}}\},\qquad 𝒟i,test={zi​j:j∈Ii,test},\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{i,\mathrm{test}}=\{z_{ij}:j\in I_{i,\mathrm{test}}\}, (10)
Ii,train∩Ii,test=∅,\displaystyle I_{i,\mathrm{train}}\cap I_{i,\mathrm{test}}=\varnothing,\qquad Ii,train∪Ii,test=Ii.\displaystyle I_{i,\mathrm{train}}\cup I_{i,\mathrm{test}}=I_{i}.

By default, the data are split once in an 80%/20% ratio. Classification datasets are stratified by the target whenever class counts permit. Generation, imputation, and prediction share the same fixed split. All model parameters, value domains, category sets, and normalization statistics are determined only from the training set. Methods that require validation data create an internal split from the training set, while the test set is reserved for final held-out evaluation.

Structural causal model evaluation set.

In addition to the OpenML evaluation set, we include the six structural causal model datasets used by TabStruct (Jiang et al., 2026): Hailfinder, Healthcare, Insurance, Magic-Irri, Mehra, and Sangiovese. Their data-generating mechanisms or variable-dependence structures are specified in advance, allowing controlled evaluation of structural recovery. These datasets are excluded from the clustering of the OpenML candidate pool and are reported separately as the structural evaluation set.

A.8 Complete Dataset Inventory

Table 6 summarizes the complete 50-dataset OpenML evaluation set and the six-dataset structural evaluation set, including their task types, sample and feature counts, variable composition, and class statistics where applicable.
