Appendix C Metric-Space Audit: Protocol and Results

Section  defines the common-support rank protocol and the criteria for retaining capability axes. Table  in the main text specifies their exact metric membership. This appendix describes the audit protocol and task-specific evidence for these choices. Appendix  defines the metrics displayed in the two rank-correlation figures.

For both generation and imputation, the mixed-type association matrix uses |r||r| for numerical–numerical pairs, Cramér’s VV for categorical–categorical pairs (Cramér, 1946), and the correlation ratio η\eta for mixed pairs (Pearson, 1905). The two tasks use different scalar summaries of this shared representation: generation reports the mean absolute difference over comparable off-diagonal pairs and its complement, whereas imputation reports the relative Frobenius distance. The metrics compare the same pairwise dependence representation but are not numerically interchangeable.

C.1 Audit protocol: common-support ranks before correlations

After constructing the ranks in Equation , the pairwise audit retains only cells in which both quantities are observed, discards strata in which either metric is constant, requires at least three methods per stratum and at least 30 paired cells over six datasets, and computes the Pearson correlation of the pooled rank pairs (the Spearman-equivalent construction used by the audit). The catalog sets ak=0.5a_{k}=0.5 for C2ST and distance-MIA AUROC and ak=0a_{k}=0 for utility gaps. The catalog marks normalized median Gower DCR as neutral; analyses that require a direction use the explicit provisional target-one transform −|x−1|-|x-1| and do not promote it to confirmatory privacy evidence. For the spectral audit, cc is the fixed metric cohort. The strata are dataset for generation, dataset–missingness setting–rate– contract for imputation, and dataset–task type for prediction. Confidence intervals use 500 bootstrap resamples (Efron, 1979) with whole datasets as the resampling units.

For relationships with finite confidence intervals, we call a pair a redundancy candidate only when its oriented correlation satisfies ρ≥0.85\rho\geq 0.85 and the 95% dataset-bootstrap lower bound is at least 0.700.70. Conversely, ρ≤−0.50\rho\leq-0.50 with an upper bound at most −0.20-0.20 marks a stable trade-off. These thresholds inform, but do not replace, semantic judgment. For the cluster counts in Table , we apply average linkage to 1−|ρ|1-|\rho| and cut at 0.150.15. This absolute-correlation clustering detects both duplicate orderings and two-sided trade-offs; only the former can be pruned. The heatmap ordering instead uses signed distance 1−ρ1-\rho so that opposing directions remain visually separate. The orderings in Figures  and display the empirical blocks; adjacency alone does not justify merging metrics.

Figures  and show the larger generation metric space separately from imputation and prediction to keep individual rank correlations legible.

C.2 From correlation blocks to redundancy clusters

Figures  and inform metric selection. Within each task, a positive block supports pooling only when its metrics share an estimand; weakly aligned metrics are not pruned and can share a named construct only as reportable complementary probes; mixed-sign blocks are retained as explicit trade-offs. The following decisions account for each pooled family and retained direction in Table .

Generation.

The full 29-metric quality audit yields 17 local correlation clusters, the largest number among the three tasks. Figure  shows the fixed 20-metric core; the full audit additionally evaluates alternate parameterizations and validity guards. The five marginal/query-fidelity metrics form the clearest positive block: pairwise correlations range from 0.8230.823 to 0.9900.990, and eight of ten pairs pass the conservative redundancy rule. An equivalent shape metric brings the cluster to six. By contrast, the two C2ST variants are only moderately aligned (ρ=0.599\rho=0.599), so linear and nonlinear distinguishability remain separate, reportable probes within the named C2ST axis rather than statistical substitutes. We pool the dense marginal/query block into fidelity, but keep α\alpha-precision, association recovery, and TSTR separate because support, dependence, and transfer are not interchangeable with marginal fidelity. Four removable generation metrics are exact alternative parameterizations; semantic review identifies only five additional metrics as substantive reductions.

A signed cluster requires separate treatment. Global utility and β\beta-recall align (ρ=0.872\rho=0.872), whereas authenticity opposes both global utility (ρ=−0.881\rho=-0.881) and β\beta-recall (ρ=−0.973\rho=-0.973). Absolute correlation therefore places them nearby, but they measure opposite ends of a support–novelty trade-off and each must remain reportable. The privacy metrics also resist reduction: mean-min Euclidean DCR has correlations of 0.4640.464, 0.6300.630, and 0.7200.720 with MIA TPR@1%, MIA AUROC, and delta presence. We group these as privacy-risk diagnostics because they provide complementary views of record proximity, membership inference, and group-presence disclosure, rather than estimates of one interchangeable quantity. None is a privacy guarantee, and exact-copy rate remains a separate memorization guardrail. These decisions yield the seven generation axes in Table .

Imputation.

The imputation panel of Figure  contains ten quality metrics in eight clusters, six of them singletons. The only stable substitutions are numerical NMAE–NRMSE (ρ=0.947\rho=0.947, 95% CI [0.931,0.959][0.931,0.959]) and categorical balanced accuracy–macro-F1 (ρ=0.925\rho=0.925, [0.899,0.949][0.899,0.949]). Point accuracy therefore does not subsume distribution matching, association recovery, or downstream utility. Missingness-shift degradation is nearly orthogonal to all level metrics, but constant imputers can appear artificially robust because their overall performance is already at a floor; we retain it as a paired diagnostic rather than a standalone ranking axis. Draw-level quantities likewise remain diagnostic rather than entering the reduced headline registry. Accordingly, Table  averages only the two point-recovery pairs and retains distribution, association, and utility as separate headline axes.

Prediction.

The prediction panels in Figure  show four observed clusters among the ten classification metrics. Hard-decision correlations range from 0.8820.882 to 0.9710.971; Brier score and log loss correlate at 0.9510.951; and correlations among ROC–AUC, average precision, and AURC range from 0.9090.909 to 0.9430.943. Accordingly, Table  pools hard decisions, proper scores, and ranking/selective risk within their respective axes, while ECE remains a singleton because calibration is not equivalent to discrimination, proper scoring, or selective prediction. In regression, RR, NRMSE, and RMSE induce almost identical method orderings (ρ>0.999\rho>0.999), MAE joins this block at the 0.850.85 cut, and median absolute error remains separate. We nevertheless report MAE independently because mean absolute and squared error encode different loss functionals. Cluster membership indicates similar rankings but does not make the estimands interchangeable. This yields four classification and three regression axes in Table .

C.3 Construct-specific stress tests

Controlled synthetic examples illustrate how selected metrics respond to specific perturbations. Independently shuffling columns preserves their marginal distributions while disrupting associations; replaying training rows can improve apparent fidelity while worsening memorization diagnostics; marginal-only imputation can approximate univariate distributions without accurately recovering individual entries or joint structure; and monotone probability rescaling can alter calibration without changing ranking. In these examples, marginal fidelity, dependence, memorization, point recovery, and calibration metrics respond differently to the imposed perturbations.

C.4 Reliability qualifies every redundancy claim

Measurement noise can obscure correlation structure or create apparent structure. Figure  therefore reports dataset- blocked rank ICC (Shrout and Fleiss, 1979) alongside two operational quantities. The separated-pair fraction counts method pairs whose replicate-mean difference exceeds 1.961.96 times the seed-level standard error of the difference; this threshold describes resolving power and is not a significance test. Top-method agreement is the mean Jaccard overlap of the best-method sets across replicate pairs. These summaries measure different properties: even a highly repeatable metric may identify different winners when several methods perform similarly. Among selected direction-defined generation components, rank ICCs range from 0.5920.592 to 0.9630.963. MIA TPR@1% and MIA AUROC form the low end at 0.5920.592 and 0.6740.674, and winner agreement can be as low as 0.1610.161. These values support retaining component-level privacy diagnostics alongside their summary. For classification, correcting correlations by the three-seed test–retest reliabilities merges hard-decision, proper-score, and ranking metrics at the same 0.850.85 cut, while ECE remains separate. We treat this correction as a sensitivity analysis rather than a mechanical selection rule: it supports one broad predictive-quality factor plus a distinct calibration direction.

C.5 Compressed, but not one-dimensional

The PCA audit (Jolliffe, 2002) uses each task’s full quality cohort. The Kaiser rule (Kaiser, 1960) retains five generation components (80% cumulative variance; PC1 53%), three imputation components (74%; 41%), two classification components (88%; 75%), and one regression component (86%; 86%). These counts are smaller than the corresponding 17/8/4/217/8/4/2 local clusters because PCA captures shared variation rather than pairwise substitutability. A dominant quality factor can coexist with a scientifically important low-variance direction such as calibration or typical absolute error.

Figure  shows a complementary spectrum for the fixed core cohorts used in the heatmaps. The participation-ratio effective rank is 3.153.15 for the ten imputation-core metrics and 2.872.87 for the twenty generation-core metrics; reaching 90% spectrum mass requires five and eight components, respectively. Classification and point regression are more compressed (1.551.55 and 1.281.28), consistent with the tight blocks in Figure . These values describe a correlation spectrum, not performance. Because pairwise correlations can use different common-support cells, the assembled matrix need not be positive semidefinite; negative eigenvalues are clipped only for this descriptive spectrum. Compression does not imply one-dimensionality: the retained semantic axes preserve stable trade-offs and distinct estimands that a purely spectral summary would blend.

Using the retained axis counts (7,6,4,3)(7,6,4,3) only as dimensionality budgets, the corresponding leading eigenspaces retain 88.22%88.22\%, 95.46%95.46\%, 96.49%96.49\%, and 99.99%99.99\% of the nonnegative spectrum for generation, imputation, classification, and regression. These are optimal same-dimensional spectral upper bounds, not the mass captured by the particular semantic composites. For the latter, let R+R_{+} denote the nonnegative-eigenvalue reconstruction of the correlation matrix and let WW encode the equal-weight composite members. We report the reconstruction fraction

𝒞⁡(W)=tr⁡[R+​W​(W​R+​W)​W​R+]tr⁡(R+),\mathcal{C}(W)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}\!\left[R_{+}W(WR_{+}W)WR_{+}\right]}{\operatorname{tr}(R_{+})}, (11)

where (⋅)(\cdot) is the Moore–Penrose inverse. The final composite spans retain 79.65%79.65\%, 86.21%86.21\%, 96.40%96.40\%, and 99.99%99.99\%, respectively. The generation value is necessarily partial: normalized median Gower DCR is neutral and therefore absent from R+R_{+}, so only the direction-defined members of the privacy-risk diagnostics axis enter this projection.

Appendix D Task Rank Analysis Details

This appendix details the procedure and aligned support for the cross-task rank analysis in Section . We compare method rankings across generation (G), imputation (I), classification prediction (P-cls), and regression prediction (P-reg). For each task pair, we restrict the analysis to the common method pool and recompute within-dataset ranks on the aligned support. This controls for differences in method availability, dataset difficulty, and metric scale.

D.1 Task Settings and Shared Support

Input units.

The input table for each task is indexed by (d,m)(d,m), where dd denotes a dataset and mm denotes a method. Each column contains one evaluation metric for that task. Raw records are first grouped using the declared seed/replicate fields and then averaged after metric orientation. Prediction datasets are separated into P-cls and P-reg according to task type. For imputation, we use the target-observed MCAR setting with a missing rate of 0.30.3.

Metric direction.

We orient metrics with a clear optimization direction so that higher values indicate better performance. We negate metrics for which lower values are better, use −|x|-|x| for metrics whose ideal value is 00, and use −|x−0.5|-|x-0.5| for metrics whose ideal value is 0.50.5. Neutral diagnostics retain their stored direction. For these diagnostics, a correlation sign describes the relation to the stored direction; it does not by itself indicate better or worse performance.

Common method pool.

For tasks aa and bb, the common method pool is defined as ℳa​b=ℳa∩ℳb\mathcal{M}_{ab}=\mathcal{M}_{a}\cap\mathcal{M}_{b}. Classification and regression use the same candidate intersections for I–P and G–P, but are analyzed independently on their respective dataset subsets. Table  reports the task-family candidate pools. We align support separately for each axis pair, retaining only dataset–method units with valid values for all declared members on both sides.

D.2 Computing Axis-Pair Correlations

Cell-wise alignment.

For capability axes (c,c)(c,c) from tasks (a,b)(a,b), let 𝒦c\mathcal{K}_{c} and 𝒦c\mathcal{K}_{c} denote their fixed member-metric sets. We define the aligned support for this axis pair as

𝒮c​c={(d,m):m∈ℳa​b,⋀k∈𝒦cvd​m​kis valid,⋀ℓ∈𝒦cvd​m​ℓis valid}.\mathcal{S}_{cc}=\left\{(d,m):m\in\mathcal{M}_{ab},\;\bigwedge_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{c}}v_{dmk}\ \text{is valid},\;\bigwedge_{\ell\in\mathcal{K}_{c}}v_{dm\ell}\ \text{is valid}\right\}. (12)

Thus, a (d,m)(d,m) unit is retained only when all declared members are valid on both sides. We construct 𝒮c​c\mathcal{S}_{cc} independently for every axis pair rather than imposing complete support across all retained axes.

Within-dataset percentile ranks.

Let ℳd,c​c={m:(d,m)∈𝒮c​c}\mathcal{M}_{d,cc}=\{m:(d,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{cc}\}. Every member metric on both sides is ranked over this same method set:

rd,m,k=rankavg⁡(vd,m,k;{vd,m,k:m∈ℳd,c​c})|ℳd,c​c|∈(0,1].r_{d,m,k}=\frac{\operatorname{rank}_{\mathrm{avg}}\!\left(v_{d,m,k};\{v_{d,m,k}:m\in\mathcal{M}_{d,cc}\}\right)}{|\mathcal{M}_{d,cc}|}\in(0,1]. (13)

Methods with identical metric values receive the average of the ranks they occupy. Percentile ranks are normalized by the size of the aligned method set and therefore lie in (0,1](0,1], with the smallest possible value equal to 1/|ℳd,c​c|1/|\mathcal{M}_{d,cc}|.

Axis aggregation.

Following Equation , the axis score is the equal-weight mean of the declared member percentile ranks:

ad,m,c=1|𝒦c|​∑k∈𝒦crd,m,k.a_{d,m,c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{c}|}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{c}}r_{d,m,k}. (14)

The member set is fixed at 𝒦c\mathcal{K}_{c}, and no additional standardization is applied after ranking. Member-complete alignment ensures that each axis score includes all its declared members.

Pooled Spearman correlation.

After constructing the axis scores, we compute

ρc​c=Spearman⁡({ad,m,c:(d,m)∈𝒮c​c},{ad,m,c:(d,m)∈𝒮c​c})\rho_{cc}=\operatorname{Spearman}\left(\{a_{d,m,c}:(d,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{cc}\},\{a_{d,m,c}:(d,m)\in\mathcal{S}_{cc}\}\right) (15)

over all units in 𝒮c​c\mathcal{S}_{cc}. This is a single correlation over the pooled dataset–method units; we do not first compute a correlation within each dataset and then average correlations across datasets. A correlation is left undefined when fewer than 10 paired units remain.

D.3 Leave-One-Method-Out Influence Diagnostics

For every method u∈ℳa​bu\in\mathcal{M}_{ab}, define the reduced method pool ℳa​b=ℳa​b∖{u}\mathcal{M}_{ab}=\mathcal{M}_{ab}\setminus\{u\}. After each removal, we recompute the aligned support, within-dataset percentile ranks, axis scores, and final correlation ρc​c\rho_{cc}. A deletion is a no-op when it changes no valid unit for that axis pair. Let ℰc​c\mathcal{E}_{cc} contain the effective deletions with finite recomputations. The LOMO sensitivity range and span are

ℛc​c=[minu∈ℰc​c⁡ρc​c,maxu∈ℰc​c⁡ρc​c],Δc​c=maxu∈ℰc​c⁡ρc​c−minu∈ℰc​c⁡ρc​c.\mathcal{R}_{cc}=\left[\min_{u\in\mathcal{E}_{cc}}\rho_{cc},\max_{u\in\mathcal{E}_{cc}}\rho_{cc}\right],\qquad\Delta_{cc}=\max_{u\in\mathcal{E}_{cc}}\rho_{cc}-\min_{u\in\mathcal{E}_{cc}}\rho_{cc}. (16)

An axis pair is called LOMO-direction-preserving when every effective recomputation has the same sign as its full-pool correlation. No-op deletions are excluded from the sign-agreement denominator and the effective deletion count. A dagger () marks axis pairs for which an effective deletion changes sign or produces zero correlation. The LOMO range is an influence diagnostic for the composition of the method pool, not a confidence interval or a significance test.

D.4 Cross-Task Axis-Level Correlations and LOMO Stability

Imputation and classification prediction (I ×\times P-cls).

Among the 24 axis pairs, 13 are LOMO-direction-preserving. Numerical point accuracy, association, and downstream utility gap have positive, direction-preserving correlations with all four classification axes. Categorical point accuracy has this relation only with hard-decision performance; neither distribution axis has a direction-preserving classification relation.

Imputation and regression prediction (I ×\times P-reg).

Fourteen of the 18 axis pairs are LOMO-direction-preserving. Numerical point accuracy, numerical distribution, association, and downstream utility gap have positive, direction-preserving correlations with all three regression axes. Categorical point accuracy also preserves a positive direction with squared error and mean absolute error, but not median error; categorical distribution is direction-unstable for all three.

Generation and imputation (G ×\times I).

Of the 42 G ×\times I pairs, 36 are LOMO-direction-preserving. TSTR gap and global-utility compromise are positive for all six imputation axes. Privacy-risk diagnostics are negative for five axes; numerical distribution is the exception. Fidelity preserves direction for five pairs, C2ST for four, and both α\alpha-precision and association for five; their signs remain axis-specific.

Generation and classification prediction (G ×\times P-cls).

Seventeen of the 28 pairs are LOMO-direction-preserving. Fidelity and C2ST are negative with all four classification axes, while TSTR gap and global-utility compromise are positive with all four. Privacy-risk diagnostics also have positive, direction-preserving correlations with proper scores. All α\alpha-precision and association pairs are direction-unstable.

Generation and regression prediction (G ×\times P-reg).

Nine of the 21 pairs are LOMO-direction-preserving. TSTR gap and global-utility compromise are positive with all three regression axes. Fidelity and C2ST are negative only against squared error, while α\alpha-precision is positive only against median error. Every association and privacy-risk pair is direction-unstable.

D.5 Complete Leave-One-Method-Out Grids

Figures – show the complete correlation grids for the full candidate pool and every LOMO recomputation. Each task pair occupies two pages for legibility. Each cell contains the pooled correlation coefficient. The grids identify which method removals account for changes in direction or large LOMO spans.

Appendix E Controlled Transfer: Protocol and Additional Diagnostics

This section expands the matched-objective study in Section . It specifies complete-member matching, inference policies, uncertainty, backbone heterogeneity, conditional interactions, and objective-arm Pareto frontiers. The implementation and re-evaluation inventory appear in Appendix .

E.1 Seven-arm member-complete construction

The intervention unit is a fixed backbone–dataset–training-seed block, with arms 𝒞={G,I,P,G​I,G​P,I​P,G​I​P}\mathcal{C}=\{G,I,P,GI,GP,IP,GIP\}. JapaneseVowels, cleveland, credit_card_clients_default, and website_phishing are classification datasets; MiamiHousing2016 is the only regression dataset. Table  gives their OpenML identifiers and fixed splits. Within each atomic setting, we orient every metric member and assign average-tie ranks across exactly the seven arms, normalized to [0,1][0,1]. Members receive equal weight within an axis, which is formed only when every declared member is finite for every arm. Imputation mechanism and rate remain separate through ranking and matching; setting-level contrasts are then averaged with equal weight. Structural applicability follows the task contract. Complete-member support is required within a backbone, not across an identical rectangle of all backbones, datasets, and seeds.

The causal population comprises Gaussian Copula, Forest-VP Joint, TabDiff, TabSyn, and TabDDPM. Forest-VP Joint uses native query-masked trees: unqueried tasks contribute neither gradients nor Hessians. GReaT is excluded from the factorial contrasts. For the four diffusion-based backbones, I and P recipients use clean observed features (x0x_{0}) when their objective is enabled and the xtx_{t} conditioning path otherwise. Gaussian Copula uses its native Gaussian conditional query in every arm. Recipient-conditioned contrasts hold the relevant rule fixed on both sides. Generation inference is fixed across arms. I/P self-inclusion and cross-arm Pareto comparisons additionally involve the policy switch in the four selector-based adapters. In G×I|PG\times I\mid P, generation and prediction rules remain fixed, but the I rule changes in those adapters when I is toggled; I-side interactions therefore cannot be attributed solely to changes in the training loss.

E.2 Uncertainty and robustness

Intervals use 2,000 crossed-bootstrap draws (Efron, 1979; Owen and Eckles, 2012), resampling backbones and datasets and then seeds within selected blocks, with all arms paired. Two-sided Wilcoxon diagnostics (Wilcoxon, 1945) use backbone–dataset means and receive Holm adjustment (Holm, 1979) within each analysis family. A robust marker requires a bootstrap interval excluding zero, adjusted p<.05p<.05, magnitude at least .05.05 rank units, all five backbones represented, at least two datasets, and non-zero backbone-specific means sharing one sign. Dataset-sign and leave-one-backbone summaries are diagnostics rather than additional gate conditions.

The analysis reports 40 off-diagonal estimates, of which 28 meet the support requirement; none passes the full gate. Of 20 self-inclusion estimates, 14 are support-eligible and 11 are robustly positive. Generation passes on fidelity, C2ST, α\alpha-precision, association, TSTR, and global utility. Imputation passes on association, categorical point accuracy, categorical distribution, numerical point accuracy, and downstream utility. Generation self-inclusion holds inference fixed. I/P self-inclusion also selects the inference policy in the four selector-based adapters and is a system-level comparison. Probability-based classification axes have only four backbones because TabDiff lacks probability outputs, while regression has only one dataset; neither group meets the full confirmatory support rule.

E.3 Utility scope and backbone heterogeneity

For P→\rightarrowG, retained TSTR is 0.092​[−0.041,0.225]0.092\;[-0.041,0.225] and global utility is −0.008​[−0.048,0.036]-0.008\;[-0.048,0.036]. A separate scope-matched per-column family yields target, all-column, and non-target effects of .069.069, −.019-.019, and −.017-.017. The direct paired localization contrasts remain unresolved: target-minus-all is 0.088​[−0.072,0.260]0.088\;[-0.072,0.260], and target-minus-non-target is 0.086​[−0.110,0.278]0.086\;[-0.110,0.278]; both have Holm-adjusted p=.133p=.133. Figure  shows the backbone variation behind pooled estimates rather than treating target alignment as an established mechanism.

Imputation mechanism and rate remain atomic throughout ranking and matching. All 144 setting-specific off-diagonal estimates fail the full robustness gate. Blank cells denote unavailable evaluations rather than zero effects.

E.4 Conditional interactions

Of 60 anchor-conditional interaction estimates, 42 meet the support rule and seven pass the gate, all negative G×I|PG\times I\mid P effects: generation association (−.315-.315), C2ST (−.393-.393), fidelity (−.468-.468), and global utility (−.154-.154), and imputation association (−.391-.391), numerical point accuracy (−.475-.475), and utility gap (−.284-.284). These describe sub-additivity under the implemented anchored systems, not independent harm from G or I or an identified optimization mechanism. Generation-side comparisons hold their evaluation rule fixed; I-side interactions additionally include the change in conditioning policy. None of the 14 support-eligible GIP-versus-singleton gaps (20 reported estimates) establishes a robust universal advantage or tax.

E.5 Complete-block Pareto analysis

The candidates are the seven arms. A task coordinate averages its declared applicable semantic axes equally; the privacy-risk diagnostic is not part of the G quality coordinate. I first averages all twelve mechanism–rate scores within each axis. The primary block analysis retains a backbone’s training-seed block only when every applicable G/I/P axis and all twelve I settings are available for all seven arms. It retains 35 classification blocks from four backbones and 12 regression blocks from five backbones. TabDiff classification is omitted from this full-axis comparison because its probability axes are unavailable. Their joint summary has 47 blocks, with seeds, then datasets within each backbone, then backbones equally weighted; it is not a common cross-backbone rectangle. Regression conclusions concern MiamiHousing2016 alone.

Exact dominance requires no loss on any task and a strict gain on one; material dominance requires no loss and a gain of at least ϵ=.05\epsilon=.05 on one coordinate. The margin does not permit a .05.05 loss on another task. Frontier membership is computed once in three dimensions, not separately in its pairwise projections. For point estimates, the exact and material sets coincide: joint {G​I,G​P,G​I​P}\{GI,GP,GIP\}, classification {G,G​I,G​P,G​I​P}\{G,GI,GP,GIP\}, and regression {G,G​I,G​P,I​P,G​I​P}\{G,GI,GP,IP,GIP\}. The joint exact-frontier bootstrap frequencies are 89.35%89.35\% for GI, 95.25%95.25\% for GP, and 98.55%98.55\% for GIP. These describe stability under resampling, not posterior optimality probabilities or significance levels. The Pareto bootstrap resamples backbones, then each selected backbone’s own datasets and seeds, preserving all-arm pairing.

E.6 Additional support checks

The available-coordinate summary in Section  retains an axis–setting coordinate when every arm is scored, without requiring the remaining axes or settings in that block. This permits TabDiff’s classification decision axis without its unavailable probability axes. A five-backbone classification check restricted to hard decisions retains 44 complete blocks and the frontier {G,G​I,G​P,G​I​P}\{G,GI,GP,GIP\}; allowing available coordinates additionally retains IP. The regression frontier is unchanged. These checks explain why the main-text view and the stricter complete-block analysis need not select identical arms.

Appendix F Fixed-Method Generality: Protocol and Additional Diagnostics

This section expands the fixed-identity deployment study in Section . Following the main-text order, it presents strict estimands and specialist references, cross-task profile geometry, and portfolio and operational diagnostics.

F.1 Strict estimands and fixed-specialist baselines

The method analysis uses the 20 semantic axes and 42 metric members specified in Table . Replicates are aggregated first; each member is oriented and converted to percentile ranks with average ties within its protocol instance; and members receive equal weight under the member-complete construction. Target-observed and feature-only imputation are never placed in one denominator. The primary imputation estimand remains separate for every mechanism–rate setting; the cross-task display coordinate is their equally weighted mean, without reranking.

A fixed specialist keeps one identity across every dataset and axis in its profile. Exact dominance is evaluated jointly in the full profile, and practical dominance permits an ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05 tolerance on every coordinate. Uncertainty is estimated using 2,000 bootstrap draws of whole datasets. Pairwise tests remove numerical ties at 1010, use a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and apply Holm correction within each declared comparison family. Frontier frequency is a stability diagnostic, not a probability that a method is optimal. The historical per-cell oracle is retained only as an unattainable reference.

The fixed-specialist pool includes ARF (Watson et al., 2023), MissForest (Stekhoven and Bühlmann, 2012), DiffPuter (Zhang et al., 2025), KNN imputation (Troyanskaya et al., 2001), MICE (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011), ReMasker (Du et al., 2024), CatBoost (Prokhorenkova et al., 2018), TabM (Gorishniy et al., 2025), LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017), and Random Forest (Breiman, 2001).

MissForest is practically stable across all numerical settings, while DiffPuter is nearly as persistent; their advantage is therefore not an artifact of one missingness regime. Categorical imputation is less uniform: MissForest remains the most persistent reference, but MICE and DiffPuter enter the frontier in setting-dependent regions. Generation results involving the normalized median Gower DCR use the provisional target-one transformation −|x−1|-|x-1| and are excluded from confirmatory privacy claims.

F.2 Cross-task profile geometry and controls

The numerical-fidelity exact frontier contains Forest-VP Joint, Gaussian Copula, LimiX-2, TabDDPM, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3, but only LimiX-2 and TabDDPM remain after the ϵ=0.05\epsilon=0.05 practical margin. The downstream-utility exact and practical frontiers both contain LimiX-2, TabDDPM, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3. These sets are computed in three dimensions; the projections above are explanatory views rather than separate frontier calculations.

F.3 Portfolio and operational diagnostics

Specialist portfolios.

The specialist portfolios in the bottom row of Figure  are the following fixed generation–imputation–prediction triples: ARF, MissForest, and LightGBM for numerical fidelity; ARF, MissForest, and CatBoost for categorical fidelity; and ARF, DiffPuter, and Random Forest for downstream utility. Each profile uses one declared triple on every dataset in its common cohort. Bootstrap intervals summarize the paired gaps over those datasets.

F.4 Interpretation rules

We use “associated” only for observational rank correlations, “transfers” only for matched objective contrasts, “dominates” only for a declared Pareto profile, and “portfolio comparison” only for the declared fixed specialist triples above. Criterion-overlap rows are retained as controls but do not count as independent cross-task evidence.

Appendix G Implementation Details

This appendix specifies the baseline settings, randomization conventions, controlled-transfer configurations, and computational environment. For benchmark implementations, method configurations, evaluation code, and installation and execution instructions, see the public OTBench repository: https://github.com/limix-ldm-ai/OTBench.

G.1 Baseline configurations and evaluation protocol

Configuration policy.

Each baseline starts from a method-specific TOML configuration, with experiment-specific overrides applied before fitting. The benchmark runners instantiate these settings directly rather than running a shared external hyperparameter search. Table 13 summarizes the principal default settings for architecture, optimization, and inference; the full method configurations are available in the public OTBench repository. HyperImpute retains its native model selection for each column and iteration. Its classifier candidates are random forest, logistic regression, XGBoost, CatBoost, and neural networks; its regressor candidates are random forest, linear regression, XGBoost, CatBoost, and neural networks. It uses ten inner iterations, lazy selection, and an optimization threshold of 1,000. It fits each incomplete evaluation matrix through its transductive fit_transform interface.

Training and validation.

The data store supplies the fixed train–test split described in Appendix . TabDDPM, TabDiff, and TabSyn use a deterministic 10% validation subset of the training rows, selected with seed 0. Their training-data view redirects any upstream training-time “test” access to this validation subset. XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, NGBoost, LightGBM-Quantile, FT-Transformer, TabM, and CARD’s guidance network use a 20% internal validation split determined by the training seed. FT-Transformer and TabM use AdamW and retain the state with the lowest validation loss; their patience is 16 epochs. MLP uses scikit-learn’s internal early-stopping split. Ridge, logistic regression, and random forest fit their training rows without an additional benchmark validation split.

Randomization and evaluation settings.

The seed set is {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}. Generation uses the same seed for training and sampling. Imputation uses paired seed tuples (strain,sselection,smask,simpute)=(s,s,s,s)(s_{\rm train},s_{\rm selection},s_{\rm mask},s_{\rm impute})=(s,s,s,s) for s∈{0,1,2}s\in\{0,1,2\}, across MCAR, MAR, MNAR, and mixed MCAR/MAR/MNAR at rates {0.1,0.3,0.5}\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}. Prediction is evaluated separately for each training seed. Training seeds and conditional-sampling draws are distinct randomization levels.

Foundation-model query interfaces.

We evaluate TabPFN-3, TabICLv2, and LimiX-2 as pretrained inference systems without dataset-specific weight fine-tuning (Grinsztajn and others, 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Zhang and others, 2026). TabPFN-3 uses the tabpfn-extensions conditional sampler for generation and imputation (Prior Labs, 2026), whereas TabICLv2 uses TabICLUnsupervised. LimiX-2 combines native feature imputation with sequential conditional generation. Prediction follows each adapter’s declared pretrained classification/regression route. A fixed method identity denotes the backbone together with its query adapters; it does not imply a shared output head. The query implementations are available in the public OTBench repository.

Resource allocation and environment.

The sharded launcher allocates one independent method–dataset worker to each visible GPU and balances datasets by (ntrain+ntest)​p(n_{\rm train}+n_{\rm test})p. Its OpenMP, MKL, and OpenBLAS thread defaults are two per worker. We use NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPUs with 32 GB of device memory per GPU.

G.2 Controlled-transfer implementation

For the underlying benchmark implementations, see the public OTBench repository. The controlled study uses the five OpenML datasets in Table , training seeds {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}, five backbones, and seven objective arms {G,I,P,G​I,G​P,I​P,G​I​P}\{G,I,P,GI,GP,IP,GIP\}. Axis scores follow the seven-arm member-complete construction in Appendix ; availability is assessed within each backbone rather than by freezing a common cross-backbone subset.

Interventions and fitting.

An enabled query type is sampled uniformly for each neural-training row, duplicated forest exposure, or Gaussian-copula optimizer update. G scores all variables; P observes the features and scores the target; I selects each feature for reconstruction with probability 0.30.3, enforces a nonempty query, and hides the target without scoring it. Observed, non-query variables form the conditioning inputs. The neural losses are masked to the queried coordinates; the forest objective sets unqueried gradients and Hessians to zero. Configurations in Table  are fixed within each backbone across datasets and arms. The three vendored neural pipelines use export protocol v6: a deterministic 10% internal holdout is drawn from the outer training split using seed 0, and training-time validation uses this holdout. TabSyn shares one objective-independent VAE per dataset–seed block across all seven arms.

TabSyn’s shared VAE selects the checkpoint with the lowest categorical cross-entropy on the internal validation set, uses ReduceLROnPlateau (factor 0.950.95, patience 10), and initializes β=10\beta=10 with decay factor 0.70.7 and threshold 1010. The causal branches bypass TabDiff’s configured plateau LR scheduler and TabSyn’s diffusion plateau scheduler and early stopping. TabDiff’s configured steps=8000 denotes epochs; TabDDPM’s steps=100000 denotes optimizer updates.

Evaluation draws and analysis.

Each checkpoint is reused for all three tasks. Generation requests as many synthetic rows as the outer training split, with evaluation seed equal to the training seed. Imputation uses MCAR, MAR, MNAR, and their mixed mechanism at rates {0.1,0.3,0.5}\{0.1,0.3,0.5\}, with the target hidden. Each mechanism–rate–training-seed setting produces three completed-table draws under one fixed, method-independent mask; the evaluation trial count is this draw count, not an additional repetition factor. Selection, masking, and imputation seeds equal the training seed. One checkpoint evaluation aggregates three conditional target draws for Forest-VP Joint, TabDDPM, TabDiff, and TabSyn; the trials and n_samples arguments do not introduce an additional nested repetition. Gaussian Copula uses native Monte Carlo budgets of 100 draws for regression and 200 for classification. Conditional sampling and training randomization are specified separately. TabDiff and TabDDPM use one imputation resampling round; TabSyn uses 50 EDM steps and 20 resampling rounds; Forest-VP uses RePaint with r=5r=5 and j=0.1j=0.1.

For Forest-VP Joint, TabDDPM, TabDiff, and TabSyn, the conditioning selector follows the training arm: prediction uses clean observed features (x0x_{0}) for P,G​P,I​P,G​I​PP,GP,IP,GIP and the xtx_{t} conditioning path for G,I,G​IG,I,GI; imputation uses clean observed features for I,G​I,I​P,G​I​PI,GI,IP,GIP and the xtx_{t} path for G,P,G​PG,P,GP. Gaussian Copula does not use this selector: it retains native Gaussian conditioning in all arms, including its Cleveland imputation re-evaluation. Recipient-conditioned contrasts therefore hold the relevant recipient protocol fixed. Generation inference is fixed across arms. I/P self-inclusion, imputation-side interactions that toggle I, and cross-arm Pareto profiles additionally compare the inference-policy switch in the four selector-based adapters.

The updated analysis reuses the completed prediction evaluations and replaces imputation outcomes with checkpoint-only re-evaluations. Of 270 planned imputation cells, 264 completed all twelve mechanism–rate settings, producing 3,168 metric artifacts. Six GPU-memory failures remain unavailable: Forest-VP Joint GI/credit_card_clients_default/seed 0; IP/JapaneseVowels/seeds 1 and 2; IP/MiamiHousing2016/seed 0; IP/cleveland/seed 0; and TabDDPM IP/credit_card_clients_default/seed 1. The old imputation outcomes for these six cells are excluded rather than mixed with the updated protocol. Other unmodified imputation baselines are retained. Re-evaluation does not update checkpoints or invoke fitting.

Uncertainty is estimated with 2,000 bootstrap draws and base random seed 20260924; 95% intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles. Point estimates average available matched settings within each seed block, then seeds within each backbone–dataset pair, and finally the pair means. Pareto point aggregation instead weights seeds, then datasets within each backbone, then backbones equally; its bootstrap resamples backbones and each selected backbone’s datasets and seeds, preserving the seven-arm pairing. Wilcoxon diagnostics use the backbone–dataset means, with Holm adjustment within each analysis family.

Appendix H Related Work

Task-specific models and benchmarks.

Generative tabular models span adversarial and variational approaches such as CTGAN and TVAE (Xu et al., 2019), language-model generators such as GReaT (Borisov et al., 2023), and diffusion methods such as TabDDPM, TabSyn, and TabDiff (Kotelnikov et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). Imputation ranges from chained equations and random forests (van Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011; Stekhoven and Bühlmann, 2012) to learned conditional models (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024). Prediction combines tree ensembles with neural and pretrained models (Chen and Guestrin, 2016; Prokhorenkova et al., 2018; Hollmann et al., 2023). Benchmark suites including Why Trees, TabZilla, TALENT, and TabArena broaden systematic comparisons for prediction (Grinsztajn et al., 2022; McElfresh et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2024; Erickson et al., 2025). These task-wise evaluations establish performance within each problem, while leaving open how capability rankings relate across generation, imputation, and prediction.

Generalist and foundation models.

Joint-distribution models can support conditional sampling, while arbitrary-conditioning approaches accommodate varied observation patterns (Ivanov et al., 2019; Jolicoeur-Martineau et al., 2024). LimiX further motivates multiple tabular queries within a shared modeling framework (Zhang and others, 2025). Recent tabular foundation models, including LimiX-2, TabICLv2, and TabPFN-3 (Zhang and others, 2026; Qu et al., 2026; Grinsztajn and others, 2026), extend the range of pretrained systems considered in our benchmark. Conditional-query extensions also expose generation and imputation routes (Prior Labs, 2026). These developments motivate distinguishing interface coverage from empirical quality under fixed model identities and task contracts. OTBench evaluates this distinction through capability-specific scores and joint task profiles, rather than introducing a new model architecture.

Evaluation and task relations.

Synthetic-data quality depends on which aspects of fidelity, dependence, and downstream utility are measured, and metrics can favor conflicting properties (Yang et al., 2024; Khan et al., 2025). Multi-task learning also studies cooperation and competition among training objectives when deciding which tasks to learn together (Standley et al., 2020). OTBench connects these issues through three complementary experiments. Task-rank analysis studies capability co-occurrence on aligned support; SAE and CAE measure objective additions and combinations under declared training–inference protocols; and fixed-method profiles compare joint task performance with specialist portfolios. This separates observational task relationships, controlled objective effects, and practical model choice, while preserving information-contract and metric distinctions.
